title: The gnome's scent trail: gone in 3.5s vs still there at 14s
question: Is 14 seconds long enough, or should a trail you walk out survive until the ants you called have been there and back (about 37s)?
context_md:
Your playtest: *"my pheramone trail should last way longer. it dissapears so much faster than an ant could even move... it should be more diffuse looking, not like a bunch of dots."*

Both halves turned out to be **one defect**. What removes a trail here is not the decay rate — it is **spreading**. Every cell bleeds a quarter of the way into its neighbours each pass, and a mark one cell wide has six empty neighbours out of nine, so it pours about **17% a pass** into bare ground while only 3% is actually being forgotten. That is also why there was no cloud to draw: a one-cell mark rounds away a cell or two out, so the picture was the spine of a cloud that did not exist.

So he now lays a **swath** at his feet rather than a dot at his chest — and it was at his chest, a body's half above the ground he had walked, which is the half no ant can ever smell.

Same walk, same ground, same seed. Both strips step 0s / 3.5s / 8s / 14s after he stops laying.

**What I am unsure of is the length, not the look.** I stopped where the swath stops paying: making it wider than this buys 4 more seconds for five times the work. Getting to a full round trip needs a different mechanic — the trail becoming a standing instruction he keeps paying power for, rather than one he lays and leaves — and that is a design decision, not a number, so I have not built it uninvited.

Nothing ant-laid was touched, per your ruling. Worth knowing for the lab: **ant trails have exactly this problem**, because the gnome's mark *was* an ant's mark — one cell, same strength. A route one scout lays and does not walk again is gone long before it can get home. What keeps ant trails alive is other ants re-walking them, and the fix there is not the decay rate either.
